Diarrhoea and Dehydration in Children
A Public Health Awareness Reference
For community health awareness use • Simple language for rural readers
Overview
Diarrhoea means passing loose or watery stools three or more times in a day. It is one of the most common illnesses in young children and is a leading cause of child sickness and death in many parts of India, including rural and tribal areas. The main danger from diarrhoea is not the loose motions themselves, but the loss of water and salts from the body, known as dehydration. Dehydration can become severe within hours, especially in small children and infants, and can be life-threatening if not treated in time. The good news is that most cases of diarrhoea can be safely managed at home with simple fluids, continued feeding, and Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS), along with quick recognition of warning signs that need medical care.
Common Symptoms
Diarrhoea and dehydration can show up in different ways. Common signs include:
Frequent loose or watery stools
Stomach pain or cramps
Nausea or vomiting
Mild fever
Weakness or tiredness
Loss of appetite
Signs that the body is losing too much fluid (early dehydration) include:
Thirst, dry mouth, or dry lips
Fewer wet diapers, or passing less urine than usual
Dark yellow urine
Reduced activity, irritability, or crying without tears
Sunken eyes
In infants, a sunken soft spot on the top of the head
Causes
Diarrhoea in children is usually caused by infections that spread through unsafe water, unwashed hands, or contaminated food. Common causes include:
Viral infections (such as rotavirus), which are the most common cause in young children
Bacterial infections from contaminated food or water
Parasites and worms, especially where sanitation is poor
Drinking unclean or unboiled water
Poor handwashing, especially before eating and after using the toilet
Unsafe food storage or spoiled food
Malnutrition, which makes children more vulnerable to infection and to severe dehydration
When to See a Doctor — Red Flag Signs
Most diarrhoea can be managed at home, but the caregiver should take the child to the nearest health centre, ASHA worker, or hospital immediately if any of the following are seen:
Blood in the stool
Repeated vomiting, unable to keep down fluids or ORS
Signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, dry mouth, no tears, little or no urine for 6 hours or more
Child is unusually sleepy, difficult to wake, or unresponsive
High fever that does not settle
Diarrhoea continues for more than 2 days without improvement
Severe stomach pain
Signs of severe weakness, fits (convulsions), or the child cannot drink or breastfeed at all
Infant below 6 months of age with diarrhoea
Child is malnourished or has an existing serious illness
If any of these signs appear, do not wait — seek medical help immediately. ORS should still be given on the way to the health facility, if the child is able to drink.
Home Care and Prevention
Home care during diarrhoea
Give ORS after every loose stool to replace lost fluids and salts.
Continue breastfeeding infants — do not stop breastfeeding during diarrhoea.
Continue feeding the child age-appropriate food; do not withhold food. Small, frequent meals are best.
Give plenty of clean fluids such as ORS, safe drinking water, and home fluids like rice water or diluted buttermilk.
Let the child rest as needed.
Wash hands with soap before feeding the child and after cleaning the child's stool.
Do not give unnecessary medicines without consulting a health worker or doctor.
Watch closely for the red-flag signs listed above.
How to prepare ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) at home
If a ready-made ORS packet from a health centre or ASHA worker is available, always prefer that — just follow the instructions printed on the packet, mixing it with the exact amount of clean water stated. If a packet is not available, a simple home sugar-salt solution can be prepared:
Wash hands well with soap and clean water.
Take 1 litre of clean drinking water (boiled and cooled, if the water source is not safe).
Add 6 level teaspoons of sugar.
Add half (1/2) a level teaspoon of salt.
Stir well until the sugar and salt fully dissolve.
Give small sips frequently using a clean cup or spoon — do not use a feeding bottle.
If the child vomits, wait 10 minutes and then continue giving small sips more slowly.
Prepare a fresh solution every day; discard any solution left over after 24 hours.
General guide for how much ORS to give after each loose stool: children under 2 years — about a quarter to half a cup; children 2 to 10 years — about half to one cup; older children and adults — as much as they will comfortably drink. The exact amount is less important than giving fluids often, in small sips, and continuing until the diarrhoea stops.
Prevention
Drink and use only clean, safe drinking water; boil water if the source is uncertain.
Wash hands with soap at key times: before eating, before feeding a child, and after using the toilet.
Use a toilet/latrine and avoid open defecation.
Keep food covered and eat freshly cooked food; avoid stale or exposed food.
Wash fruits and vegetables before eating.
Ensure children complete their scheduled vaccinations, including the rotavirus vaccine given under the national immunisation programme.
Keep the child's surroundings and drinking water storage containers clean.
Continue exclusive breastfeeding for infants up to 6 months, as advised by health workers, as it protects against infections.
Odisha-Specific Notes
In Odisha, diarrhoeal disease remains a significant concern, particularly during the summer and monsoon months, and among children in rural, tribal, and flood-prone areas where safe water and sanitation access can be limited. Families are encouraged to keep the following in mind:
Under the national Intensified Diarrhoea Control Fortnight / STOP Diarrhoea Campaign, ASHA workers pre-position ORS packets in households with children under five years — ask your local ASHA or Anganwadi worker for ORS packets and guidance.
ORS-Zinc corners are set up at health sub-centres, primary health centres, and Anganwadi centres during the campaign period; zinc supplements, along with ORS, help reduce the duration and severity of diarrhoea in children when advised by a health worker.
During and after heavy rains or flooding, take extra care with drinking water — use only boiled, chlorinated, or otherwise treated water, as flood conditions increase the risk of contaminated water sources.
Contact your nearest Sub-Centre, Primary Health Centre (PHC), Community Health Centre (CHC), ASHA, or ANM promptly if a child shows any red-flag sign, or call the Odisha health helpline / 108 ambulance service in an emergency.
Participate in local awareness activities on hygiene, safe water, and sanitation conducted by the Odisha Health and Family Welfare Department and the National Health Mission.
Source Basis
This document is based on general public health guidance and awareness materials from the World Health Organization (WHO), India's Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) and National Health Mission (including the Intensified Diarrhoea Control Fortnight / STOP Diarrhoea Campaign), the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), and related public health resources. Content has been paraphrased and simplified for general community awareness; it does not reproduce any source text directly and does not cite specific studies or documents.
Sources consulted:
World Health Organization (WHO) — general guidance on diarrhoea, dehydration, and ORS use
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India
National Health Mission (NHM), India — Intensified Diarrhoea Control Fortnight / STOP Diarrhoea Campaign
Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
Odisha Health and Family Welfare Department

This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
